passages.original: ὅτι δὲ ἀπλανῶς τάττων τὴν ιδ᾿ τοῦ πρώτου μηνὸς τῆς σελήνης ὁ Ἰσραηλίτης λαὸς ἐπιτελεῖ τὴν τοῦ πάσχα ἑορτὴν οὐ μόνον μέχρι τοῦ κυριακοῦ πάθους, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἴως τῆς ἁλώσεως τῶν Ἱεροσολύμων τῆς γενομένης ἐπὶ Οὐεσπασιανοῦ Ῥωμαίων βασιλέως, μαρτυροῦσι καὶ οἱ θεοφόροι τῆς ἐκκλησίας ποιμένες καὶ διδάσκαλοι, ἐξ ὧν ὀλίγας ἐκ πολλῶν ἐν- ταῦθα παροίσε . . . Πέτρος τῆς Ἀλε·ξανδρέων ἐκκλησίας ἐπίσκοπος ἐν τῷ περὶ τοῦ πάσχα λόγῳ, ὂν Τρικεντίῳ5) τινὶ γράφει, οὗτινος λόγου καὶ ὁ μέγας Ἀθανάσιος τῆς αὐτῆς ἐκκλησίας γενόμενος ἀρχιεπίσκοπος . . . . . . . . τῇ πρὸς Ἐπιφάνιον ἐπίσκοπον6) ἐπιστολῇ] . . . . . . . . ὧδέ πως.
passages.english: That the Israelite people, fixing without error the fourteenth [day] of the moon of the first month, celebrated the feast of the Passover not only up to the Lord's passion but also until the capture of Jerusalem that took place under Vespasian, emperor of the Romans, is attested also by the God-bearing shepherds and teachers of the Church, from whom I shall here set out a few [testimonies] out of many [...]. Peter, bishop of the church of the Alexandrians, in the discourse on the Passover which he writes to a certain Tricentius, of which discourse the great Athanasius too, who became archbishop of the same church, [...] in the letter to Bishop Epiphanius [...] [speaks] somewhat as follows.
passages.notes: The text has lacunae marked by dots; the construction is incomplete. 'ἴως' read as 'ἕως'; 'παροίσε' as 'παροίσω' (I shall set out). The superscript numbers are footnote marks and are omitted.

passages.original: Hinc deinceps terrarum orbem invasit impietas. Hic enim pravae disciplinae repertor fuit, Astrologiae scilicet ac magiae: quem et Graeci Zoroastrem appellarunt, Hunc Petrus designavit, curo ait, Post diluvium homines impie agere coeperunt.
passages.english: From then on impiety overran the world. For this man was the inventor of a corrupt discipline, namely astrology and magic; the Greeks also called him Zoroaster. Peter pointed to him when he said, "After the flood men began to act impiously."
passages.notes: The text is in Latin (a Latin version printed with the Greek), although it is labelled Greek. "curo" is read as "cum" (when). The person referred to as "this man" is not identified within the passage.

passages.original: τῆς δέ Ἀσσυρίας μετὰ τὸν Βῆλον ἐβασίλευσεν Νίνος ὁ ἄλλος υἱὸς Κρόνου, ὅστις καὶ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ μητέρα. τὴν Σεμίραμιν ἔλαβεν γυναῖκα· ἐξ οὗ Πέρσαις νόμος γαμεῖν τὰς ἑαυτῶν μητέρας καὶ τὰς ἀδελφάς, διὰ τὸ καὶ τὸν Πῖκον λαβεῖν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀδελφὴν τὴν Ἥραν γυναῖκα, καθὰ καὶ ὁ σοφώτατος Ὅμηρος ἐκτίθεται, Ἥρην προσεῖπε κασιγνήτην ἄλοχόν τε. καὶ τελευτᾷ ὁ Κρόνος. ὁ δὲ Νίνος ἐπικρατὴς γενόμενος τῆς Ἀσσυρίας κτίζει τὴν Νινευὴ πόλιν Ἀσσυρίοις, καὶ βασιλεύει πρῶτος ἐν αὐτῇ, ἔχων τὴν Σεμίραμιν τὴν καὶ Ῥέαν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ μητέρα καὶ γυναῖκα μεθ’ ἑαυτοῦ.
passages.english: After Belus, Ninus, the other son of Cronus, reigned over Assyria; he also took his own mother Semiramis as wife. From this [comes] the law among the Persians to marry their own mothers and sisters, because Picus too took his own sister Hera as wife, as the most wise Homer also sets out: "he addressed Hera, his sister and wife." And Cronus dies. Ninus, having become master of Assyria, founds the city of Nineveh for the Assyrians and reigns first in it, having with him Semiramis, also [called] Rhea, his own mother and wife.

passages.original: Assyriae vero post Belum imperavit Ninus, Saturni alius filius, qui matrem suam Semiramidem in uxorem duxit: unde Persis ex lege indultum, ut matres et sorores ducere in conjuges liceret, cum et Picus sororem Junonem matrimonio sibi pariter copulasset: quemadmodum et doctissimus Homerus ait, Junonem sororem uxoremque sic fando adortus est. Saturno extincto, Assyriae regno potitus Ninus, ac Ninive urbe exaedificata, in ea primus Assyriis imperavit, una cum Semiramide seu Rhea matre, eademque et uxore.
passages.english: After Belus, Ninus, another son of Saturn, ruled Assyria; he took his mother Semiramis as wife. Hence it was permitted to the Persians by law that they might marry mothers and sisters, since Picus too had likewise joined his sister Juno to himself in marriage: as the most learned Homer also says, "He addressed Juno, his sister and wife, speaking thus." When Saturn had died, Ninus took possession of the kingdom of Assyria and, having built the city of Nineveh, was the first to rule the Assyrians in it, together with Semiramis, or Rhea, his mother and likewise his wife.
passages.notes: This unit is a Latin version, though labelled grc.

passages.original: Ἀπήγαγεν δὲ τὴν Εὐρώπην εἰς τὴν ἰδίαν πατρίδα ὁ Ταῦρος, ἥντινα καὶ γυναῖκα ἔλαβεν οὖσαν παρθένον καὶ εὐπρεπῆ, καὶ έξλακεσε ἐκάλεσε τὰ μέρη ἐκεῖνα εἰς ὄνομα αὐτῆς Εὐρώπεια. ἐξ ἧς υἱὸν τὸν Μίνων, καθὼς Εὐριπίδης ὁ σοφώτατος ποιητὴς συνεγράψατο, ὅς φησι, Ζεὺς μεταβληθεὶς εἰς Ταῦρον τὴν Εὐρώπην ἥρπασεν·
passages.english: Taurus carried Europa off to his own homeland, and he also took her as wife, since she was a virgin and comely, and he called those regions Europe after her name. By her [he had] a son, Minos, as Euripides, the most wise poet, wrote, who says: "Zeus, changed into a bull, carried off Europa."
passages.notes: 'έξλακεσε' appears to be a garbled duplicate of 'ἐκάλεσε' and is omitted. The verb for begetting Minos is implied.

passages.original: Taurus Europam in patriam abduxit, eamque sibi conjugio sociavit, cum virgo esset et admodum formosa, vocavitque regiones illas de illius nomine Europaeas. Ex hac suscepit Minoen, quemadmodum scripsit doctissimus Poeta Euripides, cum ait, Jupiter in Taurum transformatus Europam rapuit.
passages.english: Taurus carried Europa off to his homeland and joined her to himself in marriage, since she was a virgin and very beautiful, and he called those regions European after her name. By her he had Minos, as the most learned poet Euripides wrote, when he says: "Jupiter, transformed into a bull, carried off Europa."
passages.notes: Latin text, though labelled grc.

passages.original: ἥντινα εὐθέως καταγαγὼν ἐπόμπευσεν ἐν πάσῃ τῇ χώρᾳ τῆς Αἰγύπτου, τιμωρησάμενος αὐτήν. καὶ γέγονε σωφροσύνη μεγάλη ἐν τῇ τῆς τῆς Αἰγύπτου. κἀκεῖνον δὲ τὸν μοιχὸν ἀνεῖλεν, καὶ ηὐχαριστήθη· περὶ οὗ ἱστορεῖ ποιητικῶς Ὅμηρος ποιητὴς ὡς ὁ Ἥλιος, φησίν, ἤλεγξεν τὴν Ἀφροδίτην συμμιγνυμένην νυκτὸς Ἄρει. Ἀφροδίτην δὲ ἐκάλεσεν τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν τῆς πορνείας ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἡλίου βασιλέως σοφώτατος συνεγράψατο. ἀληθές, ὡς προγέγραπται, Παλαίφατος ὁ σοφώτατος συνεγράψατο.
passages.english: He at once brought her down and paraded her through the whole land of Egypt, punishing her. And great chastity came about in the [land] of Egypt. He also killed that adulterer, and was thanked [for it]. Concerning this Homer the poet relates poetically that the Sun, he says, exposed Aphrodite lying with Ares by night. And he called the desire for fornication Aphrodite, [exposed] by King Helios. [This is] true, as written above; Palaephatus the most wise wrote it.
passages.notes: The text is disturbed: 'τῇ τῆς τῆς' is a dittography; the sentence about Aphrodite seems to have lost words and contains an intrusive 'σοφώτατος συνεγράψατο'. Translated by sense with the help of the parallel Latin.

passages.original: Lectis igitur ex castris aliquot militibus, ac observato quo per noctem adulterium committere solebat tempore, dum vir abesset, in aedes irrupit, illamque cum amasio jacentem offendit: qua confestim abrepta, ac per universam Aegyptum traducta, graviter in illam animadvertit, ex quo rite observata est deinceps apud Aegyptios castimonia, adultero insuper morte mulctato, unde a subditis gratiam iniit. Id poetico more narrat Homerus Poeta, dum ait, Venerem cum Marte noctu cubantem a Sole fuisse deprehensam. Venerem autem appellavit moechandi libidinem, quam Sol Rex prodiderit. Hujus porro historiae, quemadmodum supra relata est, veritatem descripsit doctissimus Palaephatus.
passages.english: So, having chosen some soldiers from the camp and having noted the time at which she used to commit adultery by night while her husband was away, he burst into the house and found her lying with her lover. Seizing her at once and parading her through all Egypt, he punished her severely; from this, chastity was thereafter duly observed among the Egyptians. Besides, the adulterer was punished with death, and so he won gratitude from his subjects. Homer the poet tells this in poetic fashion when he says that Venus was caught by the Sun lying with Mars at night. He called Venus the lust for adultery, which King Sol exposed. Further, the most learned Palaephatus described the truth of this story as it was related above.
passages.notes: Latin text, though labelled grc.

passages.original: καὶ ἔμειναν ἐν Πέρσιδι οἱ αὐτοὶ Σκύθαι ἐξ ἐκείνου ἕως τῆς νῦν, οἵτινες ἐκλήθησαν παρὰ τῶν Περσῶν Παρθυαῖοι, ὅ ἐστιν Περσικῇ γλώσσῃ Σκύθες, οἱ καὶ τὴν φορεσίαν καὶ τὴν λαλιὰν καὶ τοὺς νόμους Σκυθῶν ἔχουσιν ἕως τῆς νῖν, καὶ εἰσὶν μαχιμώτατοι ἐν τοῖς πολέμοις, καθὼς Ἡρόδοτος ὁ σοφώτατος ταῦτα συνεγράψατο.
passages.english: And these same Scythians have remained in Persia from that time until now; they were called by the Persians Parthians, which in the Persian language means Scythians. They have the dress, the speech and the laws of the Scythians to this day, and they are most warlike in wars, as Herodotus the most wise wrote these things.
passages.notes: 'νῖν' read as 'νῦν'.

passages.original: Ex eoque tempore Scythae illi in Perside manserunt, qui a Persis Parthidii nuncupati sunt, quod Persica lingua Scythas sonat, qui et habitum et idioma ac leges Scytharum usque nunc servant, maximeque virtute bellica praestant, quemadmodum haec tradit doctissimus Herodotus.
passages.english: And from that time those Scythians remained in Persia; they were named Parthians by the Persians, which in the Persian language means Scythians. They keep the dress, the language and the laws of the Scythians to this day, and excel greatly in warlike valour, as the most learned Herodotus relates.
passages.notes: Latin text, though labelled grc. 'Parthidii' rendered Parthians.

passages.original: τὸς Ῥοβοὰμ φαγεῖν ἄρτον, καὶ μόλις ἔφαγεν. φασὶν τὸν Ἰώσηπον λέγειν ἀπὸ παραδόσεως αἶνον εἶναι τὸν ἐν Βεθήλ, Καὶ Ὀδὴθ ἐπὶ τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου.
passages.english: [...] Rehoboam to eat bread, and he scarcely ate. They say that Josephus states, from tradition, that the one in Bethel was Ainos, and Odeth [was] at the altar.
passages.notes: Fragmentary opening ('τὸς' is the end of a lost word). The names Ainos (αἶνον, possibly a corruption) and Odeth are uncertain; apparently the two prophets of 1 Kings 13, though there the king is Jeroboam, not Rehoboam.

passages.original: et vix manducavit. Aiunt Josephum dicere, ex traditione proverbium obtinere in Bethel, Etiam Seth ad altare.
passages.english: and he barely ate. They say that Josephus states that, from tradition, a proverb prevails in Bethel: "Even Seth at the altar."
passages.notes: The passage is in Latin (a translation printed with the Greek), though labelled grc. The sense of the proverb is obscure without context.

passages.original: ἔλεον αὐτῶν ἐγκατέλιπον. ἐγὼ δέ μετὰ φωνῆς αἰνέσεως θύσω σοι, πάντα ὅσα ηὐξάμην ἀποδώσω σοι σωτήριον τῷ κυρίῳ. καὶ Προσετάγη τῷ κήτει, καὶ ἐξέβαλε τὸν ’Ιωνᾶν ἐπὶ τὴν ξηράν. Ἱστορεῖ Ἰώσηπος ἐν ἐνάτῳ τῆς ἀρχαιολογίας τὸν Ἰωνᾶν καταποθέντα R 242 ἀπὸ τοῦ κήτους ἐν τῷ Εὐξείνῳ Πόντῳ μετὰ τρεῖς ἡμέρας καὶ τρεῖς τρεῖς νύκτας ἐκβρασθῆναι η΄, θ΄, ι΄, ια΄, ιβ΄, ιγ΄. D Ἰωὰς βασιλεὺς Ἰσραὴλ συμβαλὼν τῳ ’Αμεσσίᾳ εἰς πόλεμον αἰχμάλωτον αἱρεῖ τὸν Ἀμεσσίαν, καὶ τοῦ τύχους Ἰερουσαλὴμ καθεῖλεν ὒ πήχεις.
passages.english: they have forsaken their mercy. But I will sacrifice to you with the voice of praise; all that I have vowed I will pay to you as salvation to the Lord. And it was commanded to the sea monster, and it cast Jonah out onto the dry land. Josephus records in the ninth [book] of the Antiquities that Jonah, having been swallowed by the sea monster in the Euxine Sea, was cast up after three days and three nights. [Years] 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13. Joash king of Israel, engaging Amaziah in war, takes Amaziah captive, and he pulled down 400 cubits of the wall of Jerusalem.
passages.notes: "τρεῖς τρεῖς" is a dittography, translated once. "R 242" and "D" are edition page or column marks and have been omitted. "τύχους" is read as τείχους (wall). "ὒ" is taken as the numeral υ΄ (400). The Greek numerals are year markers.

passages.original: Τὸν δὲ ἱππικὸν ἀγῶνα πρῶτος ἐπενόησεν Ἐνυάλιός τις ὀνόματι υἱὸς Ποσειδῶνος, ἀγαγόμενος τὴν Λιβύην, θυγατέρα τῆς Ἰοῦς καὶ τοῦ Πίκου Δῖός, ὃς κρατήσας τὰ μεσημβρινὰ μέρη ἐκάλεσεν τὴν αὐτὴν χώραν ἐν ᾖ ἐβασίλευσεν Λιβύην εἰς ὄνομα τῆς αὐτοῦ γυναικός. τὸν δὲ αὐτὸν ἱππικὸν ἀγῶνα ὁ Ἐνυάλιος ἅρμασι διπώλοις ἐφηῦρε, καθὼς συνεγράψατο Καλλίμαχος ὁ σοφώτατος ἐν τοῖς Αἰτησίοις αὐτοῦ. καὶ λοιπὸν μετ’ αὐτὸν ὁ ᾿Εριχθόνιος ἐπετέλεσεν καὶ ἄλλοι ἐν διαφόροις τόποις ἐπετέλεσαν. ὁ δὲ Οἰνόμαος πρῶτος αὐτὸς ἐπετέλεσεν τὸν αὐτὸν ἱππικὸν ἀγῶνα ἅρμασι τετραΐπποις·
passages.english: The first to devise the horse race was a certain Enyalius by name, a son of Poseidon. He married Libya, the daughter of Io and of Picus Zeus, and after taking control of the southern regions he called the very land in which he reigned Libya, after the name of his wife. This same Enyalius invented the horse race with two-horse chariots, as the most wise Callimachus wrote in his Aetia. And afterwards Erichthonius held it after him, and others held it in various places. But Oenomaus was himself the first to hold this same horse race with four-horse chariots;
passages.notes: "Αἰτησίοις" is presumably Callimachus' Aetia.

passages.original: Equestrium porro certaminum primus auctor fertur Enyaiius, Neptuni filius, qui ducta in uxorem Libya, Iiis et Pici Jovis filia, meridionales regiones a se subactas, de uxoris nomine Libyam appellavit. Enimvero equestres multorum curruum pugnas Enyalius adinvenit, quemadmodum doctissimus Callimachus in suis Aetesiis literis prodidit. Post Enyaliura denique Erechtonius, aliique deinceps variis in locis eosdem ludos celebrarunt. Primus autem Oenomaus certamen illud equestre quo quadrijugis bigam vehentibus dimicabatur instituit, unde celebris admodum est habitus, ut in doctissimi Characis historiis bnbetur: in quibus
passages.english: Further, the first originator of equestrian contests is said to be Enyalius, son of Neptune. Having taken to wife Libya, the daughter of Io and of Picus Jupiter, he called the southern regions he had subdued Libya, from his wife's name. Indeed, Enyalius invented the equestrian contests of many chariots, as the most learned Callimachus reported in his Aetia. Finally, after Enyalius, Erichthonius, and others in turn in various places, celebrated the same games. But Oenomaus first instituted that equestrian contest in which they competed with four horses drawing a chariot, for which reason he was held very famous, as is found in the histories of the most learned Charax: in which
passages.notes: Latin version of the preceding Greek. Scanning errors corrected: Enyaiius/Enyaliura (Enyalius), Iiis (Io), bnbetur (habetur). The Latin "multorum curruum" (of many chariots) differs from the Greek "two-horse chariots"; the translation follows the Latin.

passages.original: Circum irruit, raptasque ex gradibus puellas virgines, ac feminas quae viris carebant, sibi in conjuges adjuuxit. Hoc semel duntaxat fecit Romulus, ut doctissimus Virgilius Poeta pariter ac Apollonius Roraanae historiae scriptor, et Silvius tradiderunt. Caeteri vero historici primos Circenses ludos in raulis tum primum a Romanis actos scripsere.
passages.english: he rushed into the Circus and, seizing maiden girls from the tiers, and women who were without husbands, he joined them to himself as wives. Romulus did this only once, as the most learned poet Virgil, and likewise Apollonius, writer of Roman history, and Silvius have reported. But the other historians wrote that the first Circensian games were then held by the Romans for the first time in [...]
passages.notes: "in raulis" is unclear. It may be a corruption of "in muris" or a similar word, and has been left untranslated. "adjuuxit" is read as adjunxit and "Roraanae" as Romanae. The subject of "he rushed" is Romulus.

passages.original: Euripides moritur, ut et Sophocles Athenis.
passages.english: Euripides dies, as does Sophocles, at Athens.

passages.original: Ἐπὶ τούτων τῶν ὑπάτων Πόντιος Πιλᾶτος ἐπίτροπος τῆς Ἰουδαίας ὑπὸ Τιβερίου ἐκπέμπεται ιβ΄ ἔτει τῆς βασιλείας αὐτοῦ, ὡς ἱστόρει Ἰώσηπος.
passages.english: Under these consuls Pontius Pilate is sent out by Tiberius as procurator of Judaea, in the twelfth year of his reign, as Josephus recorded.

passages.original: LIII. Zenas, Jurisperitus; quorum Paulus meminit in Epistola ad Philemon.
passages.english: 53. Zenas, the lawyer; of these Paul makes mention in the Epistle to Philemon.
passages.notes: The text is in Latin. The plural "quorum" (of whom) suggests the entry once listed more names, or that it is copied from a list of several names. Zenas is actually named in Titus 3:13, not in Philemon.

passages.original: LVI. Demas, quorum meminit Paulus in Epistola ad Philemonem.
passages.english: 56. Demas, of whom Paul makes mention in the Epistle to Philemon.
passages.notes: The text is in Latin. It has the plural "quorum" (of whom), as in the preceding entry.

passages.original: Sanctus Joannes Praecursor et Baptista capite truncatur ab Herode Rege Judacae, primi Herodis filio, Archelai iratre: cum vinctus in Macherunta castrum missus fuisset propter Herodiadem: de quo meminit sacra Bvangeliorum scriptura. Narrat autem Josephus libro XVIII. Antiquitatum Judaicarum, ut
passages.english: Saint John the Forerunner and Baptist is beheaded by Herod, king of Judaea, son of the first Herod and brother of Archelaus, after he had been sent in chains to the fortress of Machaerus on account of Herodias; this is mentioned by the sacred scripture of the Gospels. And Josephus relates in Book 18 of the Jewish Antiquities how
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: Judacae, iratre, Bvangeliorum.

passages.original: Herodiadem porro a conjuge adhuc in vivis divulsit, ob quam Joannem sustulit. Herodi vero bellum intulit Aretas, ob injuriam filiae illatam, quo in bello universum Herodis exercitum profligatum, idque ob structas Joanni insidias esse passum aiunt. Idem denique Josephus refert ob Herodiadem regno excidisse Herodem, illumque cum ea relegatum, Lugduni Hispaniae urbe habitare jussum, cum summus esset Pontifex Simon Camathi filius.
passages.english: Further, he separated Herodias from her husband while [the husband] was still alive, and on her account he did away with John. Aretas made war on Herod because of the wrong done to his daughter, and they say that in this war Herod's whole army was routed, and that he suffered this because of the plot laid against John. Finally, the same Josephus reports that Herod lost his kingdom on account of Herodias, and that he was banished with her and ordered to live at Lugdunum, a city of Spain, when Simon son of Camathus was high priest.
passages.notes: "Lugdunum of Spain" stands as written in the text.

passages.original: ipso vero die lunae habentis xin. hora nocturna v. illucescente in xxiv. regnante Herode Tetrarcha, ut indicat Lucas Evangelista Extincto enim Herode, qui infantes sustulerat, in ejus filios regnum est devolutum, ut narrat Josephus, factusque est Rex Judaeae Archelaus, qui annos ix. regnavit. Post illius vero mortem, Herodes Tetrarcha ejus frater regnavit in Galilaea annos xxiv. usque ad mortem Tiberii. Porro Judaeae Pontius Pilatus imperabat.
passages.english: and on that very day, the moon being 13 [days old], at the fifth hour of the night, dawning into the 24th, while Herod the Tetrarch was reigning, as Luke the Evangelist indicates. For when Herod, who had killed the infants, had died, the kingdom passed to his sons, as Josephus relates, and Archelaus became king of Judaea, who reigned 9 years. After his death, Herod the Tetrarch, his brother, reigned in Galilee 24 years, until the death of Tiberius. Pontius Pilate, moreover, governed Judaea.
passages.notes: "xin" is read as xiii (13). The construction of the dates is elliptical.

passages.original: Ἰησοῦς ὁ Χριστὸς ἀνελήφθη εἰς τοὺς οὐρανοὺς τῇ τρίτῃ τοῦ ἀρτεμισίου μηνὸς ἐν ἡμέρᾳ πέμπτῃ τῆς ἑβδομάδος, καὶ καθὼς γέγραπται, Ἀνάστηθι, κύριε, εἰς τὴν ἀνάπαυσίν σου σὺ καὶ ἡ κιβωτὸς τοῦ ἁγιάσματός σου. καὶ ὁ ἅγιος Ἀθανάσιος ἑρμηνεύων τὸν ρλα΄ ψαλμὸν ἔγραψεν οὕτως· „Ἀνάστηθι, κύριε, εἰς τὴν ἀνάπαυσίν σου· τὴν εἰς οὐρανοὺς ἀνάληψιν ἐπισπεύδουσιν αὐτοῦ. Σὺ καὶ ἡ κιβωτὸς τοῦ ἁγιάσματός σού τὴν ἁγίαν αὐτοῦ σάρκα φησί· μετ’ αὐτῆς γὰρ ἀνελήφθη. οὐ γὰρ ἀποσαρκοῦται εἰς τοῖς ἀγηράτους αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων.“
passages.english: Jesus the Christ was taken up into the heavens on the third of the month Artemisius, on the fifth day of the week, and as it is written, "Arise, Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your holiness." And the holy Athanasius, interpreting the 131st psalm, wrote thus: "'Arise, Lord, into your rest': they are urging on his ascension into the heavens. 'You and the ark of your holiness': he means his holy flesh, for he was taken up with it. For he is not stripped of the flesh into the ageless ages of ages."
passages.notes: ρλα΄ = 131 (Psalm 132 in English numbering). "εἰς τοῖς" read as "εἰς τοὺς".

passages.original: His Coss. Pontius Pilatus Christianorum dogmata Tiberio Caesari, ille vero Senatui Romano communicavit. Senatu autem id non admittente, Tiberius capitis poenam in Christianorum delatores decrevit, quemadmodum Tertullianus Latinus scriptor refert.
passages.english: In this consulship Pontius Pilate reported the teachings of the Christians to Tiberius Caesar, and he communicated them to the Roman Senate. But when the Senate did not accept this, Tiberius decreed the death penalty against those who informed against the Christians, as Tertullian, the Latin writer, reports.
passages.notes: This passage, though labelled Greek, is in Latin (from the Latin version printed with the edition).

passages.original: Caius Caesar simul ac imperare coepit, Herodem propter Herodiadem in exilium misit, ut ait Josephus, et Agrippam vinculis solutum Judaeorum Regem constituit: (hic est Herodes qui Jacobum interfecit, de quo loquuntur Acta Apostolorum, a pediculis consumptus) qui annos VII. regnavit, Caio
passages.english: As soon as Gaius Caesar began to rule, he sent Herod into exile on account of Herodias, as Josephus says, and released Agrippa from his chains and made him king of the Jews (this is the Herod who killed James, of whom the Acts of the Apostles speak, [and who was] consumed by lice), who reigned seven years, under Gaius
passages.notes: Latin text. The passage breaks off mid-sentence and continues in the next unit.

passages.original: quidem iv. Claudio vero post Caium imperante annos m. ut scribit Josephus.
passages.english: four, and under Claudius, who ruled after Gaius, three years, as Josephus writes.
passages.notes: Latin text. "m." is probably a scanning error for "iii." (3 + 4 = 7, as the previous unit gives); translated as three.

passages.original: Nec multo post: Illo tempore injecit Herodes manusf ut quosdam affligeret de Ecclesia, et interfecit Jacobum fratrem Joannis gladio, et Petrum misit in custodiam. Quae cum fecisset Herodes, statim moritur, a vermibus consumptus, scribente Josepho eum annis vii. regnasse.
passages.english: Not long after: "At that time Herod laid hands on some of the Church to afflict them, and he killed James the brother of John with the sword, and put Peter in custody." When Herod had done these things, he immediately died, consumed by worms, Josephus writing that he reigned seven years.
passages.notes: Latin text. "manusf" read as "manus" (stray footnote mark).

passages.original: Ab assumptione enim Domini, usque ad hanc profectionem, complentur Apostolorum anni xiv. et menses x. Quod si hoc non demus, invenietur tempus a quo baptizatus est, et visum recepit, ut Acta continent, annorum iv. Et hoc non solum ex Actis colligitur, sed etiam ex Josepho, scribente ad tertium Claudii annum vitam produxisse Herodem: statimque post mortem Herodis, ad Apostolatum
passages.english: For from the Lord's assumption up to this journey, fourteen years and ten months of the Apostles are completed. But if we do not grant this, the time from when he was baptized and received his sight, as the Acts contain, will be found to be four years. And this is gathered not only from the Acts but also from Josephus, who writes that Herod prolonged his life to the third year of Claudius; and immediately after Herod's death, to the apostolate
passages.notes: Latin text. Breaks off mid-sentence.

passages.original: usque ad annum quo a Felice in carcerem conjectus est, cum sub Nerone Romam esset mittendus, ut deinceps Acta enarrant, annique imperii (Claudii) rursum evincunt. Postea veniens Hierosolyma cum Barnaba, ibique invento Petro, caeterisque Apostolis, cum Jacobo fratre Domini, epistolam scribunt Apostoli Antiochiam Syriae, ut Ecclesiae suae fundamenta jacerent, quam Paulus ipse et Barnabas Antiochiam deferunt, ut habent Acta. Ex hoc plane colligitur Apostolos Catholicas suas Epistolas scripsisse, antequam ii dispergerentur, quantumvis Petrus, ut quidam volunt, solus ipse Roma scripserit. Quin et Matthacus primus ibi Hierosolymis, ut ait Chrysostomus, Evangelium scripsit. Arbitror autem . . . Hic una
passages.english: …up to the year in which he was thrown into prison by Felix, when he was to be sent to Rome under Nero, as the Acts go on to relate, and as the years of the reign (of Claudius) again prove. Afterwards, coming to Jerusalem with Barnabas, and finding Peter and the other apostles there, together with James the brother of the Lord, the apostles write a letter to Antioch in Syria, so that they might lay the foundations of its church; Paul himself and Barnabas carry it to Antioch, as the Acts have it. From this it is plainly gathered that the apostles wrote their Catholic Epistles before they were dispersed, however much Peter, as some hold, wrote alone from Rome. Indeed Matthew too first wrote his Gospel there in Jerusalem, as Chrysostom says. But I think . . . Here together…
passages.notes: The text is in Latin. The passage begins in mid-sentence and breaks off after "Arbitror autem" ("But I think"), followed by a gap; the closing words "Hic una" are an incomplete fragment. "Matthacus" is read as "Matthaeus" (Matthew). In "Ecclesiae suae fundamenta jacerent" (literally "lay the foundations of its church"), the reference of "suae" is uncertain.

passages.original: Agebatur tum Paschatis dies, cum urbem Hierosolymitanam expugnavit, et undecies centena Judaeorum millia, iis gladio interemptis, delevit, aliaque centum quinquaginta millia captivorum ex adolescentibus et pueris, ac virginibus et puellis, sub corona vendidit, ut tradit Josephus doctissimus Chronographus: quippe ut Hebraeus belio isti interfuit. Judaeae porro provincias omnes vastavit Titus.
passages.english: It was then the day of the Passover when he took the city of Jerusalem by storm and destroyed one million one hundred thousand of the Jews, slaying them with the sword, and sold into slavery another hundred and fifty thousand captives from among the youths and boys, and maidens and girls, as Josephus, a most learned chronographer, relates; for as a Hebrew he was present at that war. Furthermore Titus laid waste all the provinces of Judaea.
passages.notes: Latin text. "belio" read as "bello".

passages.original: Refert Josephus lib. v. de excidio Hierosolymitano, contigisse Judaeorum expugnationem anno III. Vespasiani, post XL. scilicet annum, ex quo in Jesum aggressi sunt facinus: quo tempore, inquit, et Jacobum fratrem Domini Hierosolymorum Episcopum ab ipsis praecipitem ex alto actum, et lapidibus appetitum, sustulere.
passages.english: Josephus reports in book 5 on the destruction of Jerusalem that the conquest of the Jews took place in the third year of Vespasian, that is, after the fortieth year from when they committed their crime against Jesus; at which time, he says, they also did away with James, the brother of the Lord, bishop of Jerusalem, who was thrown headlong from a height by them and attacked with stones.
passages.notes: Latin text.

passages.original: Ad hunc annum Philo et Josephus historias suas perduxerunt, in quibus narrant excidiuiu Hierosolymitanum.
passages.english: Philo and Josephus carried their histories down to this year, in which they narrate the destruction of Jerusalem.
passages.notes: Latin text. "excidiuiu" read as "excidium".

passages.original: ζεται τὴν νῆσον, ἔνθα τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν ἑωρακέναι λέγεται, ὡς δηλοῖ Εἰρήναιος.
passages.english: [...] the island, where he is said to have seen the Revelation, as Irenaeus shows.
passages.notes: Begins mid-word ("-ζεται", perhaps from a verb such as "is exiled to" / "inhabits"); the opening is lost.

passages.original: est relegatus, ubi Apocalypsin vidisse dicitur, ut Irenaeus tradit.
passages.english: was banished, where he is said to have seen the Apocalypse, as Irenaeus relates.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the subject (presumably John, banished to Patmos) is not in the text. This unit is the Latin version printed alongside the Greek.

passages.original: Ἰνδ. τγ΄.δ΄. ὑπ. Τραϊανου Αὐγούστου τὸ γ΄ καὶ Πέτου. Ἰωάννην τὸν ἀπόστολον καὶ εὐαγγελιστὴν μέχρι τῶν Τραϊα- νοῦ χρόνων παραμεῖναι τῷ βίῳ Εἰρήναιος ἱστορεῖ. Κλήμης δὲ ὁ Ἀλεξανδρεὺς καὶ αὐτὸς τὰ αὐτὰ σύμφησι, καὶ περιιέναι αὐτὸν τὴν Ἀσίαν καὶ τὰς πλησιοχώρους πατρίδας ἐπισκἱπους καθιστῶντα καὶ κληρικούς.
passages.english: Indiction 13, [year] 4. Consulship of Trajan Augustus for the 3rd time and of Paetus. Irenaeus records that John the apostle and evangelist remained alive until the times of Trajan. Clement of Alexandria also says the same things, and [says] that he went about Asia and the neighbouring regions, appointing bishops and clergy.
passages.notes: The numerals 'τγ΄.δ΄' are garbled in the scan. I have read them as indiction 13, year 4, but this is uncertain. 'ἐπισκἱπους' is a scanning error for ἐπισκόπους (bishops).

passages.original: Joannem Apostolum et Evangelistam ad tempora Trajani vitam produxisse scribit Irenaeus. Clemens vero Alexandrinus iisdem consona tradit, iliumque Asiam et finitimas provincias peragrasse, Episcopis ubique ordinatis, ac Clericis constitutis.
passages.english: Irenaeus writes that John the Apostle and Evangelist prolonged his life to the times of Trajan. Clement of Alexandria relates things consistent with these, and [says] that he travelled through Asia and the neighbouring provinces, ordaining bishops everywhere and appointing clergy.
passages.notes: Latin version of the preceding Greek. 'iliumque' is a scanning error for 'illumque'.

passages.original: Κέρδων τῆς κατὰ Μαρκίωνα πλάνης ἀρχηγός, ποτὲ μὲν συνὼν τοῖς ἐν Ῥώμῃ χριστιανοῖς, ποτὲ δὲ παραδιδάσκων καὶ λέ-
passages.english: Cerdo, the originator of the error of Marcion, at times associating with the Christians in Rome, at times teaching otherwise and say-
passages.notes: The text breaks off mid-word ("λέ-", say-).

passages.original: Hoc anno Apelles et Aristo, quorum meminit in sua Historia Ecclesiastica Eusebius Pamphili, librum apologeticum pro religione nostra Hadriano Imperatori porrigunt.
passages.english: In this year Apelles and Aristo, whom Eusebius Pamphili mentions in his Ecclesiastical History, present an apologetic book on behalf of our religion to the emperor Hadrian.
passages.notes: Eusebius in fact names Quadratus and Aristides as the apologists to Hadrian; the names 'Apelles et Aristo' may be a corruption.

passages.original: Valentini et Marcionis haereticorum sectatoribus sano Christi verbo convertit. Is Marcioni aliquando sibi in faciem occurrenti, ac dicenti, Agnoscis nos? respondit, Agnosco te primogentitum Satanae, quemadmodum narrat Irenaeus.
passages.english: [...] converted [many] of the followers of the heretics Valentinus and Marcion by the sound word of Christ. Once, when Marcion met him face to face and said, 'Do you recognise us?', he replied, 'I recognise you, the firstborn of Satan,' as Irenaeus narrates.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the subject is presumably Polycarp. 'sectatoribus' should probably be 'sectatores', or an object such as 'multos' has been lost. 'primogentitum' is a scanning error for 'primogenitum'.

passages.original: Ἐπὶ τούτου Ἡγήσιππος τελειοῦται περὶ τῶν ἀποστόλων με- γάλως συγγραψάμενος, ὡς ἱστορεῖ Εὐσεβίος Παμφίλου.
passages.english: Under him Hegesippus died, having written magnificently about the apostles, as Eusebius Pamphili records.

passages.original: Illo imperante, decessit Hegesippus, qui de Apostolis magnifice scripsit, ut testatur Eusebius Pamphili.
passages.english: While he was reigning, Hegesippus died, who wrote magnificently about the apostles, as Eusebius Pamphili testifies.

passages.original: οὐκ εὐτονούντων τῶν δημίων εἰς τοσοῦτον ἀπειρότατον πλῆθος ἐξαρκεῖν. περὶ τούτου τοῦ ἀπείρου πλήθους τῶν μαρτυρησάντων Λουκιανὸς πρεσβύτερος Ἀντιοχεῦσι γράφων ἐδήλου, Ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς χορὸς ἅπας ὁμοῦ μαρτύρων. εὐαγγελίζομαι δέ ὑμᾶς ὡς Ἄνθιμος ὁ πάπας τῷ τοῦ μαρτυρίου δρόμῳ ἐτελειώθη. καὶ τὰ μὲν κατὰ Νικομήδειαν ταῦτα καὶ τούτων ἔτι πλείονα. Ἰνδ. η΄. κ΄ .
passages.english: [...] since the executioners did not have the strength to cope with so utterly boundless a multitude. Concerning this boundless multitude of those who were martyred, Lucian the presbyter made it known when writing to the Antiochenes: 'The whole chorus of martyrs together greets you. And I bring you the good news that Anthimus the bishop has been perfected in the course of martyrdom.' These, then, were the events at Nicomedia, and still more than these. Indiction 8, [year] 20.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence. 'πάπας' (literally 'pope' or 'father') is here used of the bishop of Nicomedia.

passages.original: Idem hic Praepositus Rhodanus viduae cuidam Berenicae, potentia sua fretus, bona per calumniam eripuit: illa vero cum Valentinianum Imperatorem contra Praepositum actura adiisset, ille Salustium Patricium iis dedit judicem, a quo Rhodanus est condemnatus. Imperator, ut decretum Salustii Patricii intellexit, praecepit Rhodano Praeposito, uti quae viduae rapuisset restitueret. Verum Rhodanus adduci non potuit, ut quae viduae abstulerat redderet, sed a Salustio Patricio provocavit.
passages.english: This same Rhodanus, the Praepositus, relying on his power, seized by false accusation the property of a certain widow, Berenice. When she approached the emperor Valentinian to take action against the Praepositus, he gave them the patrician Salustius as judge, by whom Rhodanus was condemned. When the emperor learned of the decision of the patrician Salustius, he ordered Rhodanus the Praepositus to restore what he had seized from the widow. But Rhodanus could not be brought to return what he had taken from the widow; instead he appealed against the patrician Salustius.
passages.notes: *Praepositus* is a court office, the chamberlain (praepositus sacri cubiculi).

passages.original: sustulit, quod idem Amantius Imperatorem Theocritum facere in animo habuisset, datis ipsi Justino pecuniis, quas erogaret ut Theocritus ille Imperator fieret. Atque revera is pecunias dedit: verum iis acceptis, Praetoriani, plebsque, posthabito Theocrito, ipsum Justinum creavere Imperatorem. Postquam igitur Imperator factus est, illos tanquam tyrannos, quique imperio suo insidias struerent, interfecit.
passages.english: [...] removed [them], because this same Amantius had intended to make Theocritus emperor, having given Justin himself money to distribute so that this Theocritus might become emperor. And indeed he did give the money; but once they had received it, the praetorian guards and the people passed over Theocritus and made Justin himself emperor. So after he had become emperor, he put them to death as usurpers who were plotting against his rule.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence, so the subject and object of 'sustulit' are missing.

passages.original: per partes a se invicem separantur ea, ex quibus Dominus noster Jesus Christus compositus est, differentiam tamen considerantes et hanc significare voientes, numerum assumimus, et duas in Christo naturas esse di- cimus: nec ideo unus Christus in duos Christos, vel in duos filios dividitur. Et testimonium praestat nostris dictis Sanctus Gregorius Theologus, scribens in primo libro ad Cledonium sic: Si quis introducit duos filios, unum quidem ex Deo et Patre, secundum autem ex matre, sed tre non unum eumdemque, ex adoptione cadat, quae promissa est recte credentibus.
passages.english: …the elements from which our Lord Jesus Christ is composed are separated from one another into parts; yet, considering the difference and wishing to signify it, we adopt number and say that there are two natures in Christ. Nor is the one Christ on that account divided into two Christs or into two sons. And Saint Gregory the Theologian bears witness to our words, writing thus in his first book to Cledonius: "If anyone introduces two sons, one from God and the Father, and a second from the mother, and not one and the same, let him fall from the adoption which has been promised to those who believe rightly."
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence. Though labelled Greek, it is a Latin version of the text. "sed tre non" is evidently a garbled "sed non". Other scanning errors have been corrected silently: "voientes" for "volentes" and "di- cimus" for "dicimus".

passages.original: οὐδέ γὰρ εἶνναι λέγει τὸν Χριστὸν θεόν, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπὶ τῷ παραδόξῳ τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἐκπλαγέντα τὸν Θωμᾶν ὑμνῆσαι τὸν θεὸν τὸν ἐγείραντα τὸν Κριστόν. τὸ δὲ χεῖρον, ὅτι καὶ ἐν τῇ τῶν Πραξέων τῶν ἀποστόλων γενομένῃ παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ δῆθεν ἑρμηνείᾳ συγκρίνων ὁ αὐτὸς Θεόδωρος τὸν Κριστòν Πλάτωνι καὶ Mανιχαίῳ καὶ Ἐπικούρῳ καὶ Μαρκιωνι λέγει ὅτι ὡσπερ ἐκείνων ἕκαστος εὑράμενος οἰκεῖον δόγμα τοὺς αὐτῷ μαθητεύσαντας πεποίηκε καλεῖσθαι Πλατωνικοὺς καὶ Μανιχαίους καὶ Ἐπικουρείους καὶ Mαρκιωνιστάς, τὸν ὅμοιον τρόπον καὶ τοῦ Κριστοῦ εὑραμένου τὸ δόγμα ἐξ αὐτοῦ τοὺςχριστιανοὺς καλεῖσθαι.
passages.english: For he says that Christ is not God, but that Thomas, astounded at the marvel of the resurrection, praised the God who raised Christ. And what is worse, in the supposed interpretation of the Acts of the Apostles produced by him, this same Theodore compares Christ to Plato, Mani, Epicurus and Marcion, and says that just as each of them, having devised his own doctrine, caused those who became his disciples to be called Platonists, Manichaeans, Epicureans and Marcionists, in the same way, Christ having devised the doctrine, Christians are called after him.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "εἶνναι" is read as "εἶναι", and "Κριστόν" as "Χριστόν". "For he says": the subject is probably Theodore reporting Thomas's words, though the sentence is loosely constructed.

passages.original: Sed et confessionem, quam fecit Thomas cum palpasset manus et latus Domini post resurrectionem, dicens: Dominus meus, et Deus ωευε, inquit non esse dictam a Thoma de Christo, (nec enim dixit Theodorus Deum esse Christum) sed ad miraculum resurrectionis stupefactum Thomam glorificasse Deum,qui Christum resuscitavit. Et quod pejus est, etiam in interpretatione quam in Actis Apostolorum scripsit Theodorus, similem fecit Christum Platoni, et Manichaeo, et Epicuro, et Marcioni, dicens quod sicut illorum unusquisque ex dogmate quod invenit, suos discipulos fecit vocari Platonicos, et Manichaeos, et Epicureos, et Marcionistas, simili modo et cum Christus dogma invenisset, ex ipso Christianos vocari.
passages.english: And he also says that the confession which Thomas made when he had touched the hands and side of the Lord after the resurrection, saying, "My Lord and my God," was not said by Thomas about Christ (for Theodore did not say that Christ is God), but that Thomas, astounded at the miracle of the resurrection, glorified God, who raised Christ. And what is worse, even in the interpretation which Theodore wrote on the Acts of the Apostles, he made Christ like Plato, Mani, Epicurus and Marcion, saying that just as each of them, from the doctrine he devised, caused his disciples to be called Platonists, Manichaeans, Epicureans and Marcionists, in the same way, when Christ had devised a doctrine, Christians are called after him.
passages.notes: The text is in Latin. The scanning error "ωευε" is read as "meus" (my).

passages.original: Ipsis enim Arianis ad decipiendos populos suo errori conjungentibus Dionysium, qui ante multos annos Athanasii fuit Alexandriae Episcopus, et dicentibus quod et ipse Dionysius similia eis sapuit, Athanasius magnus Ecclesiae Doctor multis modis ostendit in scriptis, rectam fidem Dionysium ab initio praedicasse, nulloque modo participem Arianae impietatis fuisse. Isti autem haeretica sapientes, suam impietatem eidem Synodo applicare festinant.
passages.english: For when the Arians themselves, in order to deceive the people, linked to their error Dionysius, who many years before Athanasius was bishop of Alexandria, and said that Dionysius too held views like theirs, Athanasius the great Doctor of the Church showed in many ways in his writings that Dionysius had preached the right faith from the beginning and had in no way shared in the Arian impiety. But these men, who hold heretical views, hasten to attach their own impiety to that same Synod.
passages.notes: The text is Latin despite the Greek language label.

passages.original: συνόδου, καθὰ μαρτυρεῖ ὁ ἐν ἁγίοις Ἀθανάσιος. ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ ἐν χαλκηδόνι ἁγία σύνοδος Δόμνον τὸν Ἀντιοχείας γενόμενον ἐπίσκοπον μετὰ θάνατον κατεδίκασεν, τολμήσαντα μόνον γράψαι δεῖν παρασιωπηθῆναι τὰ ιβ΄ κεφάλαια τοῦ έν ἁγίοις Κυρίλλου. ἐπειδὴ δὲ οἱ Θεοδώρου ἀντιποιούμενοι αἱρετικοὶ πάσης προτάσεως γαῖ ἐγγυήσεως ἐκπεπτωκότες ἐπεχείρησαν λέγειν πρὸς ἀπάτην τῶν ἀγνοούντων ὡς ὁ τῆς ὁσίας μνήμης Κύριλλος ἔν τινι μέρει ἐπιστολῆς τοῦτον ἐπῄνεσεν, ἐκ πολλῶν ἀποδεικνυται ὅτι οὔ συμβαίνει τὸ αὐτῶν ἐγχείρημα τοῖς εἰρημένοις παρὰ τοῦ ὲν ἁγίοις Κυρίλλου ἐν διαφόροις αὐτοῦ λόγοις κατὰ τοῦ δυσσεβοῦς Θεοδώρου, ἐν οἷς ἀσεβέστερον αὐτὸν πάντων τῶν ἄλλων αἱρετικῶν ἀποδείξας, εἶτα οὐκ ἐνεγκὼν τὸ πλῆθός τε κα μέγεθος τῶν αὐτοῦ βλασφημιῶν τῶν εἰρημένων κατὰ τοῦ μεγάλου θεοῦ καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἀπεφθέγξατο οὕτως εἰπών, Ἐξέστη ὁ οὐρανὸς ἰπὶ τούτῳ καὶ ἔφριξεν ἐπὶ πλείω σφόδρα, λέγει κίριος.
passages.english: …synod, as Athanasius among the saints testifies. But the holy synod at Chalcedon also condemned Domnus, who had been bishop of Antioch, after his death, because he had dared only to write that the twelve chapters of Cyril among the saints ought to be passed over in silence. And since the heretics who champion Theodore, having failed in every argument and every guarantee, have attempted to say, to deceive the ignorant, that Cyril of holy memory praised him in some part of a letter, it is shown from many [passages] that their attempt does not agree with what was said by Cyril among the saints in his various discourses against the impious Theodore. In these he showed him to be more impious than all the other heretics; then, unable to bear the multitude and magnitude of his blasphemies spoken against our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, he burst out, saying: "The heaven was astonished at this and shuddered exceedingly, says the Lord."
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence. "γαῖ" is read as "καὶ", and "κα" as "καὶ". The quotation echoes Jeremiah 2:12.

passages.original: censi Synodo, prout testatur Sanctus Athanasius. Sed et Caichedonensis sancta Svnodus Domnum Antiochiae factum Episcopum post mortem condemnavit, quod solum ausus est scribere, oportere taceri duodecim capitula Sancti CyriJli. Quoniam autem Theodori defensores haeretici, omni propostione et conatu excidentes, praesumunt dicere ad deceptionem ignorautium, quod Sanctae metnoriae Cyrillus in aliqua parte epistolae illum collaudavit;
passages.english: …synod, as Saint Athanasius testifies. But the holy Synod of Chalcedon also condemned Domnus, who had been made bishop of Antioch, after his death, because he had dared only to write that the twelve chapters of Saint Cyril ought to be kept silent. And since the heretical defenders of Theodore, failing in every proposition and attempt, presume to say, to deceive the ignorant, that Cyril of holy memory praised him in some part of a letter…
passages.notes: The passage is a Latin version and breaks off mid-sentence. The opening "censi" is the end of a word, probably "Nicaenae" or a similar adjective. Many scanning errors have been corrected silently.

passages.original: καὶ τοῦτο δείκνυται ἐκ διαφόρων αὐτῶν λόγων τε καὶ ἐπιστολῶν πρὸς Θεοδόσιον τὸν τῆς εὐσεβοῦς λήξεως καὶ ἑτέρους διαφόρους γραφεισῶν. καὶ ταῦτα μὲν οὕτως. ἵνα δὲ μηδὲν τῆς ἀκριβείας πάρα λείψωμεν, ἀναγκαῖον ἐνομίσαμεν μνησθῆναι καὶ τῶν γραφέντων παρὰ Αὐγουστίνου τοῖ τῆς ὁσίας μνήμης ἐπισκόπου ἐν Ἀφρικῇ γενομένου. ζητήσεως γάρ τινος περὶ Καικιλιανοῦ μετὰ θάνατον αἰτοῦ κινηθείσης, ὡς τῆς ἐγ̣γ· λrσιαστιγ̣ῆς παρατραπέντος παραδόσεως, καί τινων τούτου χάριν χωρισάντων ἑαυτοὺς τῆς καθολικῆς ἐκκλησίας, γράφει πρὸς Βονιφάτιον ὁ αὐτὸς τῆς ὁσίας μνήμης Αὐγουστῖνος ὡς οἰκ ἔδει τινὰς διὰ τοῦτο χωρίσαι ἑαυτοῖς τῆς καθολικῆς ἐκκλησίας·
passages.english: And this is shown from their various discourses and letters written to Theodosius of pious end and to various others. So much for this. But so that we may omit nothing of exactness, we thought it necessary to mention also what was written by Augustine of holy memory, who was a bishop in Africa. For when a certain inquiry was raised about Caecilian after his death, on the grounds that he had departed from the ecclesiastical tradition, and some for this reason had separated themselves from the catholic church, the same Augustine of holy memory writes to Boniface that some ought not for this reason to have separated themselves from the catholic church:
passages.notes: The garbled "ἐγ̣γ· λrσιαστιγ̣ῆς" is read as "ἐκκλησιαστικῆς" (ecclesiastical).

passages.original: Ut autem nihil subtilitatis praetermittamus, necessarium putavimus memorare etiam illa, quae ab Augustino sanctae memoriae Africano Episcopo scripta sunt. Quaestione enim aliqua post mortem Caeciliani de eo mota, quod ab Ecclesiastica traditione declinasse dicebatur, et propter hoc quibusdam a Catholica Ecclesia separatis, scribit ad Bonifacium idem Sanctus Augustinus, quod non oportebat, aliquos ideo separare sese a Catholira Ecclesia: Si enim vera essent ea quae Caeciliano inferebantur, et manifestatus esset contrarium aliquid Ecclesiastico statui sapuisse, etiam post mortem cum anathemati subjicerem.
passages.english: But so that we may omit nothing of precision, we thought it necessary to mention also what was written by Augustine of holy memory, an African bishop. For when some question was raised after Caecilian's death concerning him, because he was said to have departed from ecclesiastical tradition, and some had on this account separated from the Catholic Church, the same Saint Augustine writes to Boniface that some ought not for that reason to separate themselves from the Catholic Church: "For if the things charged against Caecilian were true, and it had been made clear that he held something contrary to the Church's position, I would subject him to anathema even after his death."
passages.notes: The text is Latin. "cum" is read as "eum" (him). The Latin has the first person "subjicerem" ("I would subject"), whereas the Greek has the third person plural "they would have subjected".
